titleStmt.title: Integrating Cyber-Attack Defense Techniques into Real-Time Cyber-Physical Systems

analytic.title: Integrating Cyber-Attack Defense Techniques into Real-Time Cyber-Physical Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: With the rapid deployment of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), security has become a more critical problem than ever before, as such devices are interconnected and have access to a broad range of critical data. A well-known attack is Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) which can diverge the control flow of a program by exploiting the buffer overflow vulnerability. To protect a program from ROP attacks, a useful method is to instrument code into the protected program to do runtime control flow checking (known as Control Flow Integrity, CFI). However, instrumented code brings extra execution time, which has to be properly handled, as most CPS systems need to behave in a real-time manner. In this paper, we present a technique to efficiently compute an execution plan, which maximizes the number of executions of instrumented code to achieve maximal defense effect, and at the same time guarantees real-time schedulability of the protected task system with a new response time analysis. Simulation-based experimental results show that the proposed method can yield good quality execution plans, but performs orders of magnitude faster than exhaustive search. We also built a prototype in which a small auto-drive car is defended against ROP attacks by the proposed method implemented in FreeRTOS. The prototype demonstrates the effectiveness of our method in real-life scenarios.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In recent years, we witness a boost in the deployment of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) as a result of the rapid development of Internet and embedded computing technology. CPS can sense the state of physical world and transfer the sensing data to almost anywhere as the CPS components are typically interconnected. This trend has created a broad range of application domains which brings unprecedented convenience to human life, such as smart city, smart grid, smart factory, and all kinds of smart personal devices. However, such systems are now severely exposed to security threats as they are highly interconnected. Security problems have become much more critical than ever before. SANS cybersecurity report shows that 54% of industry control systems have suffered 1-5 severe attack incidents per year and almost all industry control systems have experienced attacks to some degree [1]. In uncovered attacks, Stuxnet virus propagates across the network and is believed to be responsible for causing substantial damage to Iran's nuclear program [2].

Among the different types of cyber-attacks, a very dangerous one is the Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) attack ‡ Corresponding author: lumingsong@cse.neu.edu.cn. The paper is supported by the National Science Foundation of China under Grant 61772123, 61532007, 61602104 and the Ministry of Education Joint Foundation for Equipment Pre-Research under Grant 6141A020333. which exploits buffer overflow vulnerability. This vulnerability has been a severe security threat to computer systems for nearly 30 years. MITRE lists it as the top three most dangerous software errors [3] and ICS-CERT lists it as the most common vulnerability in Industrial Control Systems [4]. ROP attacks try to divert the control flow of a program by overwriting a return address or a function pointer. In theory, turing completeness ability can be achieved by ROP attacks [5], by which attackers can manipulate the physical components of a CPS. In real attack scenarios, to elude the Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS), the attacker typically does not change the system state dramatically [6]. For example, a car traveling on a flat road can hardly make a 90-degree turn in a few milliseconds, and it can only be deviated from the road little by little. This makes such attacks even harder to detect. Control Flow Integrity (CFI) [7] is proposed as an effective defense technique to ROP attacks, which instruments code into the original program so that control flow integrity check can be performed at run-time.

In reality, most CPS are essentially hard real-time (HRT) systems in which each task must finish before its specified deadline. Although instrumenting security check code can effectively defend a system against ROP attacks, the instrumented code introduces extra execution time to the system, especially when the tasks require frequent executions. As reported in related work, CFI-like techniques will introduce about 3% -20% execution time overhead [8], which has a significant impact on the schedulability of a system. So there is a challenge to integrate defense techniques into HRT systems without affecting the schedulability of the protected system.

In this paper, we studied the problem of integrating instrumentation-based defense techniques into real-time systems. A technique is presented to efficiently compute an execution plan, which maximizes the number of executions of instrumented code to achieve maximal defense effect, and at the same time guarantees real-time schedulability of the protected task system. Simulation-based experiments are conducted, which show that the proposed method can yield good quality execution plans with very low analysis time. We also implemented the proposed method to defend a prototype auto-drive car against ROP attacks, which demonstrates that our method is effective in real-life scenarios.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, we present the system model applied in our research. The instrumentation planning methods as well as the system implementation are presented in Sec. III. In Sec. IV, the effectiveness of our method and the schedulability affected by a defense technique are evaluated. A prototype is also built and tested in Sec. V. Related works are presented in Sec. VI and the paper is concluded in Sec. VII.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL A. Attack and Defense
div.p: IDS, which detects cyber attacks based on system behavior, has been widely deployed in complex CPS. However, it can be easily bypassed by attackers [9]. Hence it is crucial to detect attacks from the perspective of program execution. Stack Cookies, Data Execution Prevention, Address Space Layout Randomization, etc., are typical techniques for attack defense of computer systems [10]. However, for the sake of cost and execution efficiency, none of the above defense techniques are used in MCU-based embedded systems [9]. Moreover, C/C++ language, which is prone to memory leaks, is often used in such devices, which makes cyber attacks easier and more dangerous.

In this study, we aim at systems vulnerable to ROP attacks and focus on CFI or more general code instrumentation based defense techniques. Such defense techniques detect attacks by setting check points before program jump instructions and checking whether the target address conforms to the original control flow.

Actual security checks are performed if the instrumented code is executed. In this work, we can control the execution of instrumented code in the operating system. It should be noted that our model is not restricted to CFI; it is applicable to any mechanism that brings extra execution time to the program, including static and dynamic instrumentation, checking control flow and checking control variables [11].

We assume that the system adopts a Simplex-like architecture [12] which includes a safety subsystem and a complex subsystem. In normal execution, the system executes the complex subsystem and may be attacked. Once anomaly is detected, execution is switched to the safety subsystem immediately and may only perform basic functions to avoid further attacks.

div.head: B. Real-Time Task Model
div.p: We consider a HRT system with a real-time task set Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n } running on a single processor with fixed priority real-time scheduling. A task τ i is said to have a higher priority than task τ k if i < k. A task τ i ∈ Γ is described by a set of parameters (C i , T i , D i , O i , SL i ), where:
• C i is the worst execution time (WCET); • T i is the period of the task; • D i is the relative deadline of the task, and in this research
div.formula: D i = T i ; • O i is

div.head: the execution time bound of a security check;
div.p: • SL i is the security level of the task (a smaller SL i indicates a higher security level). In real systems, the overhead O i differs with the applied defense technique and the specific task. It is generally believed that the overhead is proportional to the execution time of a task [8], i.e., O i = γC i , where γ > 0. In this work, we assume that all the security checks take the worst-case time overhead.

Security level is very similar to the concept of criticality level in mixed-criticality systems [13], which is an independent dimension other than task priority to specify the security property of a task. It is typically assigned by system designers according to the vulnerability and the criticality of a task.

div.head: III. OUR APPROACH
div.p: In this section, we first explain how the execution time overhead of security check can be considered in the wellknown response time analysis. Then two methods on how to plan the execution of security check are presented: Exhaustive Search (ES) and Security-Level Monotonic (SLM). Finally, an illustrative example is presented.

Among all the jobs of a task, we select a subset of jobs to execute security checks and keep the other jobs unchanged. This process constructs an execution plan, and the following factors need to be considered:

1) The existing scheduling strategy should not be changed since it is carefully designed for the target application and the schedulability of the task set has been verified; 2) Checking for high security level tasks should be prioritized since malfunction of a high security level task may lead to catastrophic consequences; 3) The execution plan should be efficiently computed and adapt to timing jitters, for the sake of realistic implementation in real systems.

div.head: B. The Exhaustive Search Algorithm
div.p: To achieve the best defense effect, the objective is to maximize the number of executions of security check. A straightforward way is to exhaustively enumerate all possible execution plans within a hyper-period of the task set.

The algorithm starts from the task with the highest security level (line 19), and for each job released by the task in the hyper-period (line 2), tries to execute security check (line 12). Once a new state is obtained, a simulation is performed to check whether the task system is still schedulable (line 13) in the presence of the execution time overhead of security checks. This process works recursively until all tasks are analyzed in the order of security level.
Although the ES algorithm can produce optimal results, it has two major shortcomings.

First, the critical instant for single-processor response time analysis (where all tasks start simultaneously leads to the worst case) [14] no longer holds in the presence of security checks. This phenomenon is illustrated by Example 1. For the given task set Γ, if τ 1 and τ 2 start simultaneously at time 0, the ES algorithm executes security check at the second and the third job of τ 1 without compromising the schedulability, as shown in Figure 1a. If τ 1 arrives 1 time unit later than τ 2 , the execution plan produced by the ES algorithm no longer applies, as the second job of τ 2 will miss its deadline, as shown in Figure 1b. This phenomenon brings two major adverse effects: 1) other time-consuming analyses, such as simulation of the scheduling in one hyper-period, have to be adopted to check schedulability; 2) once task release time is changed (timing jitters), a new search has to be done from scratch.

div.head: C. The Security Level Monotonic Algorithm
div.p: Due to the above shortcomings, the ES algorithm cannot be used in real-life scenarios. In practice, we need a method which can efficiently and systematically compute execution plans and work on a critical instant to simplify schedulability test and adapt to timing jitters. Thus, we proposed the Security Level Monotonic (SLM) algorithm.

The basic idea of SLM is that we can establish a critical instant considering the time overhead of executing security checks. With the critical instant: 1) execution plan can be computed efficiently and systematically; 2) response time analysis can now be applied to ensure the schedulability of a task set (although some pessimism may be introduced).

We first consider assigning security checks for a single task and conducting schedulability analysis for one low priority task. Later, the result will be extended to multiple tasks. If a higher priority task τ h is considered, we need to compute the interference suffered by lower priority tasks. To achieve this, we show that Theorem 1 holds.

div.head: D. Implementation
div.p: In order to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method in real-life systems, we implemented the new scheduler as well as a simple ROP attack and CFI defense on FreeRTOS.

a) Scheduler: We modified the kernel code of FreeRTOS to dynamically trigger security check. The major function is to record the number of executed jobs, and to decide if a security check should be executed according to the execution plan. APIs were designed to allow user to specify the protected tasks and the execution plan that is computed offline.

b) Attack: In ROP attack, attackers construct a gadget chain to operate maliciously, which contains some gadgets linked with RET instruction, i.e., a previous gadget will jump to the next gadget when the RET instruction is executed. As illustrated in Figure 3, two gadgets are constructed. Gadget1 is used to modify stack pointer to the start address of local variable that contains addresses of other gadgets. Gadget2 is used to execute malicious code, and return to the function invocation point. The payloads (are sent by attacker) exploit the buffer-overflow vulnerability of C programs which allows the size of variable to exceed allocated space. To evade exception of stack overflow, we construct two payloads. The first one executes Gadget1 and Gadget2 and returns to the function invocation point. At this time, the stack pointer is advanced 8 bytes compared to the initial state. The second payload only executes Gadget2 and the stack pointer is restored. Using the two payloads alternatively can execute malicious code without causing any exception. c) Defense: We used shadow stack as a simple CFI defense technique to protect a program against stack-based attacks, by instrumenting the checking code into program with GCC. As illustrated in Fig. 4, a shadow stack is created in a reserved safe memory area. When a function is invoked, the instrumented code saves return address in both the normal In this section, we use randomly generated task sets to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method and how security checks affect the schedulability of the system. We generated 800 task sets and organized them into 10 groups according to total processor utilization. The utilization of the i-th group is [0.01 + 0.1 • i, 0.1 + 0.1 • i], 0 ≤ i ≤ 9, and each task set contains [3,10] tasks. The period of each task is T i ∈ [10ms, 100ms], which is randomly generated using a uniform distribution. The processor utilization U i for each task is generated using the UUniFast algorithm [15], and the execution time of a task is generated using
div.formula: C i = U i • T i .
div.p: Rate Monotonic scheduling is adopted. All the experiments are conducted on a desktop computer with Intel Core i7-4770 CPU and 16GB memory. The CBC ILP solver [16] is adopted for the SLM algorithm.

div.head: A. Effectiveness
div.p: The overall goal of this work is to maximize the defense effect efficiently, and we assume the more security checks an algorithm can assign, the better the defense effect. To evaluate the effectiveness, we aim to compare SLM with ES (which produced optimal results) in terms of both defense effect and computation efficiency.

To evaluate defense effect, let m s hp (A) denote the number of security checks that algorithm A can assign in a hyper-period, and we introduce a concept defense efficiency, denoted by η, defined as follows:
div.formula: η = m s hp (SLM ) m s hp (ES)(9)
div.p: Clearly, the closer the ratio is to 1, the higher the efficiency of the SLM algorithm. As the ES algorithm needs to enumerate all possibilities in one hyper-period, which is very timeconsuming, we limit the hyper-period of generated task set to be less than 300 and set m s i = m i for the SLM algorithm. We set the overhead to 3% and 20% respectively (which is a relatively reasonable range [8] [17]). For security levels, two settings were explored: 1) the security level order is the same as the priority order (the "coincide" bars in Figure 5a); 2) the security level order is set reversed to the priority order (the "reverse" bars in Figure 5a).

The results of defense efficiency is shown in Figure 5a, which are organized according to the total utilization of the task set from 0.6 to 1.0 (different column sets along the xaxis). For each utilization, we report the efficiency value for both the two overhead settings and the two security level settings.

For task sets with low total utilization, for example 0.6, SLM can achieve the same defense effect as ES (efficiency is 1). As the utilization increases, the defense effect of SLM decreases, which is more prominent in cases the overhead is high (20% in the experiment). However, the efficiency value is still above 60% even for the worst case (the utilization is 0.9 and the overhead is 20%). For task sets in which the security level order is set reversed to the priority order, the efficiency is worse. The main reason is that in this setting, the frequently executed high-priority tasks are at low security levels so that they are less likely to be defended.

We also evaluated the computation efficiency of SLM and ES. The results are reported in Figure 5b. The analysis time of the ES algorithm can reach up to 199s and increases significantly with the utilization. However, the SLM algorithm performs much more efficiently than ES. As can be seen, the analysis time of SLM is 0.05s on average, and more importantly, it does not increase much with the utilization. Also note that from the principle of the ES algorithm, the analysis time will increase exponentially with the hyperperiod, rendering it to be infeasible in practice. SLM does not suffer this problem as the state space is greatly restricted due to the established critical instant and the value of m s i to balance between defense effect and computation efficiency.

div.head: B. Schedulability
div.p: We also aim to evaluate how the defense technique affects the schedulability of a task system. To show this, we compute the percentage of schedulable task sets in different total utilization and different execution time overhead of security checks, as reported in Figure 5c. 0% overhead means no security check, and this case can be used as a baseline for comparison. When the utilization is below 0.6, the slack time is enough for security checks, so the schedulability is almost not affected. As the utilization increases and goes beyond 0.8, the schedulability degrades significantly. Even 3% overhead can cause a 19% decrease in schedulable rate. The results indicate that the execution time overhead of security checks has adverse effect to the schedulability of a real-time system, and thus security checks have to be enabled very carefully and safe schedulability test should be conducted to ensure the real-time requirements are still satisfied.

div.head: V. CASE STUDY
div.p: As the efficiency value to evaluate the SLM algorithm in the previous section is not intuitive to show the actual defense effect in real-life scenarios, we also built a small car platform to verify the effectiveness of SLM, shown in Figure 6. The control board is a STM32F1 MCU based embedded device. The application scenario is to let the car follow a predefined track with the help of a CCD camera mounted. The control board is also equipped with an NRF24L01P 2.4G wireless communication module to enable the car to communicate with external world. The simulated attacks are also injected via this wireless communication port. FreeRTOS is modified and runs on the device. Five tasks are designed to control the car, their functionalities and parameters are given below.
• τ comm : receives wireless data and stores it in a buffer.
• τ ccd : reads the camera data.
• τ ctl : reads the buffer data.
• τ pwm : modify the kinematic parameter of the car.

• τ show : updates the on-car display. To implement a ROP attack, we exploit the buffer overflow vulnerability of a task, i.e., τ ctl did not check its length when reading a packet to a local variable. The attack is designed to let the car turn right to go off track. The steering of the servo motor of front wheel can be controlled by modifying the pulse width stored in the CCR register, and the car will go straight if the CCR value is 1500 or turn right if the value is greater than 1500. In the attack design, the CCR value is adversely modified to 1744, and the attack period is the same as the period of victim task τ ctl . To defend, when an attack is detected by the shadow stack technique, task τ ctl will discard packets tempered by the attacker, and the car is only navigated by the camera. But the communication channel continues to read new packets, which makes further attacks possible. In the experiments, we evaluated the defense effect with different total utilizations (88.7%, 83.2%, 76.9%) by adjusting the task periods (three periods settings: T H i , T M i , T L i ). The car's cruise track on a straight segment is represented by the CCR values. As shown in Figure 7, we generated two attacks within 100ms. Without defense technique, the car will The results show that our proposed method can efficiently defend the demo system against ROP attacks and at the same time guarantee the schedulability of a task system. Similar results can be witnessed for all the three utilization settings.

div.head: VI. RELATED WORK
div.p: In the past decades, research in the real-time community has been focused on guaranteeing schedulability of a task. As realtime systems are intensively interconnected than ever before, they are highly exposed to cyber attacks. Thus it is crucial to defend such systems against various attacks and at the same time to guarantee schedulability.

Related research was conducted to defend real-time systems from leaking critical information due to resource sharing, for example, data stored in shared cache. Mohan et al. in [18] and Pellizzoni in [19] proposed techniques to execute extra code to purge the shared cache between task switching boundaries where information leaking is possible. The execution time overhead has been included in the schedulability analysis of the protected system.

Another form of attacks to real-time systems is to analyze the task execution patterns so that specific task can be identified as the attack target, and the attacker may set up timing side channels to collect information. Techniques were proposed in [20] [21] to defend a real-time system against such attacks by shuffling the execution of tasks so as to disturb timing inference by attackers. However, such techniques are not able to defend systems against ROP-like attacks.

Providing defense to real-time systems for external attacks can be classified into two main categories: system-level defense task and task-level defense. For the first class, one or more tasks specifically designed to detect attacks and provide protections were added to the task system [22] [23]. A major challenge is to select proper periods of such tasks to balance between defense effect and the extra interferences introduced into the system. However, such techniques are not able to defend a system against ROP-like attacks which try to divert the control flow of a specific task.

For task-level defense, researchers have proposed some hardware-based techniques. In [24] [25], special hardware was designed to detect process malfunctions by analyzing the execution time properties of processes. CFI defense techniques were also implemented on hardware [26] [27] to protect a task against ROP-like attacks by analyzing jump instructions, with the objective to minimize detection and protection overhead. However, most COTS processors do not integrate such functions, so the applicability of hardware-based defense is very much limited.

Two existing research practices are closely related to our work. In [28], a technique was proposed to provide security service for each job of a task. The main problem studied is how to combine multiple services to improve defense effect while maintaining schedulability. However, it may leave critical tasks unprotected when integrating a specific technique. In [29], a task-level defense technique was proposed to protect a realtime system from man-in-the-middle attacks. The optimization target is set to maximize the Quality-of-Control for control tasks. Our proposed technique focuses on code instrumentation to general tasks and thus may be applied to a broader range of real-time applications.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: With the ever increasing degree of connectivity for realtime CPS devices, cyber attack has become a very critical issue. This paper presents a method to integrate defense techniques (at the task/program level) into real-time systems. The proposed method is able to efficiently find a sub-optimal plan to execute instrumented security check code for the protected tasks/programs so as to achieve the best defense effect while guaranteeing schedulability of the system. Both simulation-based experiments and an implementation of the proposed method on a auto-drive car prototype show that the proposed method can be used to achieve the design target of securing real-time CPS systems.
